expertise_required.why: Classification of the software (EAR99 vs 5D002/ENC vs USML XI if adapted for military sensors) and cap-table structure for SBIR must be settled before approaching DoD.

regulatory_burden.explanation: The unclassified ATAK-CIV/open-data product is likely commercial software (EAR99, or 5D002 with License Exception ENC if it ships encryption - RECALL, verify with counsel); no ATO is needed for public-safety pilots on agency-run TAK Servers, though state programs may require their own review. Burden rises to medium if the product is adapted for military sensors or distributed as a TAK-MIL plugin (TPC review; possible USML Category XI questions) and to high only if it were pulled into classified integration, which this scope excludes.
regulatory_burden.non_us_person_founder_note: In the unclassified public-safety form the Indonesian founder can participate fully in engineering. Constraints appear at the defense boundary: SBIR ownership/control test, AFWERX foreign-national limits, TAK-GOV/MIL distribution control, CUI/OWT data access, and any future facility clearance (FOCI review under 32 CFR 117). These need export-control, SBIR and DCSA counsel; no legal determination is made here.

dual_use_potential.explanation: Wildfire, SAR, disaster response, border and infrastructure-inspection users on TAK are real and offline-first has appeal; but the same users have shown they adopt free stacks (ATAK + UAS Tool + MediaMTX) and cloud mapping bundled with their drone platform (Skydio, DJI, DroneSense), so willingness to pay for a standalone plugin is unproven.

defensibility.explanation: Algorithms (ODM, Obj2Tiles, change detection) are open; interfaces (KLV, CoT, 3D Tiles, GeoPackage, TAK SDK) are open or government-controlled; data is open; there are no network effects in a plugin. The only accumulable assets are tuned change-detection thresholds from real flights, a deployed base of agency TAK Servers, and TPC/agency relationships - a head start, not a moat.

card.why_now: Since 2023: Jetson Orin-class edge compute makes minute-scale reconstruction feasible; the Army standardised on a KLV/CoT-emitting company-level drone (Skydio X10D) and DFR programs expanded drone flying in public safety; TPC is adding Cesium 3D Tiles to TAK and AGC is standardising basemap packages (2025-2026); OWT production (Vantor, Feb 2026) multiplies the 3D data that must reach edge devices; NGC2/DDIL requirements were written down. But the same changes let Skydio, Reveal and TPC ship the capability themselves, which they have.
card.killer_risk: The product's headline function (KLV to georegistered footprint) is already a free government plugin, its second function (minute-scale 3D on a commodity box) is a stock feature of the Army's chosen drone and the product of a funded, acquisitive competitor with ATAK export, and its third and fourth functions (edge change overlays, priority delta of terrain packages) are increments on roadmaps owned by TPC, AGC, Reveal and Ditto - with no requirement owner, no budget line and a public-safety buyer whose revealed price for the surrounding stack is zero. It is a feature set inside a government-owned, services-priced ecosystem, not a company.

card.allied_extension: Only marginally. Allied and coalition TAK users (UK, NATO SOF, Australia) and German civil-protection agencies sit outside NGC2 and could be a channel for the German founder, and allied civil users are less exposed to the SBIR ownership problem; but they inherit the same free ATAK/UAS Tool baseline, the same Skydio/Reveal/DJI alternatives, and TAK-MIL distribution control applies to them too. Public evidence on German or NATO civil TAK adoption at scale is insufficient. The allied angle changes the sales channel, not the feature-versus-company problem.

score.title: Drone-agnostic sensor-to-map TAK plugin (MISB KLV to georegistered footprints, incremental 3D Tiles and change-vs-baseline overlays on a commodity edge box) with bandwidth-budgeted delta distribution of terrain and basemap packages across TAK federations

scores.rationale: The headline pain (seeing where the drone camera is looking on the TAK map) is already solved for free by ATAK plus the government UAS Tool plugin (FACT, MEDIUM). What remains - waiting hours for cloud 3D when offline without a Skydio/Reveal licence, judging change by eye, stale terrain packages - is real but the corpus and this session's searches found no primary-source AAR or solicitation naming it; the sneakernet-terrain pain was still HYPOTHESIS/LOW after G03's two passes.

Drone flights are daily in DFR programs, wildfire seasons and company sUAS teams, so any residual friction recurs often; but the residual functions (change alerts, terrain refresh) are needed episodically, not on every flight.

No budget line names a sensor-to-map plugin or geospatial delta distribution (Public evidence insufficient). Adjacent money is prime-shaped (AIDP-Next, TITAN, OWT data buy) or program-internal (DHS S&T TAK, TPC). Public-safety users have revealed a zero price point by adopting the free ATAK + UAS Tool + MediaMTX stack. A 1 rather than 0 because SBIR/STRATFI has funded the adjacent product (Reveal) and DHS S&T does pay integrators for TAK features.

ATAK-CIV and TAK Server source are open and a community plugin can be distributed without any contract, so access to users is easy; but there is no office that buys plugins (TPC approval-gated, services-priced), SBIR carries the ownership test, and Army entry runs through AIDP-Next/NGC2 primes.

Every component is open or commodity: MISB KLV parsers, OpenDroneMap/Obj2Tiles to 3D Tiles (FACT, HIGH), Jetson Orin, TAK SDK, CRDT/chunk-manifest sync. The hard parts (incremental reconstruction speed, low-false-alarm change detection, priority scheduling) are engineering, not research.

$250k comfortably buys the unclassified PoC ($60-150k) and a first pilot attempt, but not a defense-validated demo (TAK-GOV/MIL access, exercise participation, clearable field engineer) and not the photogrammetry hire plus 18 months of runway needed to find a paying customer in a free ecosystem.

A lab demo (any KLV feed -> 3D Tiles in minutes -> change overlay -> delta-synced across two federated TAK Servers over a 64 kbit/s emulated link) is achievable in 3-6 months on open data and commercial hardware. Not a 5 because 'credible' for a buyer requires a live user pilot, which needs a sponsor.

Open terrain (USGS 3DEP, Copernicus), open imagery, self-flown KLV video, ATAK-CIV and TAK Server public source cover the entire MVP. Military FMV and OWT are not needed unless the defense variant is pursued, where they are sponsor-gated.

The civil ATAK-CIV product is likely commercial software (EAR99 or 5D002/ENC - RECALL, verify with counsel) with no ATO for agency-run pilots; the defense variant brings TPC MIL-plugin review, possible USML XI questions if adapted for military sensors, and TAK-GOV/MIL distribution control. Medium overall.

A 5 because the scope is unclassified by construction: commercial drones, open data, public TAK source, public-safety first customers; classification dependence is 'none' and no controlled data is required for any MVP milestone.

A 1 because every layer has a free, stock or funded occupant: government UAS Tool (KLV footprint, free), Skydio Onboard Modeling (stock on the Army's company drone), Reveal Farsight (edge 3D to ATAK, USSOCOM-developed, $33.6M STRATFI + $30M Series B, acquisitive), Edgybees (georegistration), OpenDroneMap (free algorithms), DroneSense/DJI/Vision2 (public-safety TAK video), Ditto/CloudTAK/map-depot/AGC RBT (distribution). Only the change-overlay and priority-delta increments are unoccupied.

A 1 because the principal incumbent is government-owned free software with a live roadmap (Cesium 3D Tiles program and AGC RBT demo on the TAK Offsite 2026 agenda, FACT HIGH); it cannot be undercut on price, and the commercial occupants (Skydio, Reveal) are well funded and closer to the users than a new entrant.

Interfaces are open standards (KLV, CoT, 3D Tiles, GeoPackage) and ATAK-CIV SDK is public, but every interface is controlled by someone else (TPC, AGC, drone vendors, Cesium), MIL plugin approval is gated, and the 2026 WinTAK-to-TAKX migration creates maintenance churn.

A 1 because algorithms, interfaces and data are all open and the parent cards' own defensibility sections reach the same conclusion; the only accumulable assets (tuned thresholds, deployed agency servers, TPC relationships) are a head start any of the named incumbents can erase in one or two release cycles.

Wildfire, SAR, disaster, border and inspection TAK users are real and offline-first has appeal, but they already use free stacks and vendor cloud mapping; willingness to pay for a standalone plugin is unproven.

Could expand to allied TAK federations and to more sensor types, but each expansion is another feature inside the same free ecosystem; the realistic ceiling is an Immersive Wisdom-scale niche (single-digit $M/yr, INFERENCE).

Public-safety subscriptions and allied support contracts could recur, but military TAK users do not pay licence fees for plugins and the free baseline erodes renewal leverage; services renewals are the realistic form.

The unclassified scope lets both founders engineer, and the German founder's allied channel is a small plus; but three 'fatal if absent' roles (photogrammetry engineer, TAK ecosystem engineer with TPC relationships, public-safety/SOF domain seller) are missing, SBIR is blocked until the cap table is restructured, and neither founder has flown drones under TAK for a living.

market.summary: No requirement owner, program office or budget line for a sensor-to-map plugin or geospatial delta distribution; the PROBLEM -> USER -> REQUIREMENT OWNER chain breaks at REQUIREMENT OWNER (TPC/AGC/DHS S&T own the roadmap, nobody owns this feature) and at BUDGET (Public evidence insufficient). Public-safety users have revealed a zero price point for the surrounding stack (free ATAK + UAS Tool + MediaMTX); Army money is prime-shaped (AIDP-Next, TITAN, NGC2). Residual pains (change alerts, terrain freshness) remain HYPOTHESIS/LOW after three research passes across G13, G03 and G31. TAK plugin economics are services-shaped (PAR acquired by Booz Allen). Analyst assessment: ACCEPTED; the only soft spot is that DHS S&T does fund TAK features through integrators, which supports a consultancy path, not a company.

competition.summary: The first named function is a free government plugin (UAS Tool shows footprint/SPI from KLV), the second is stock on the Army's company-level drone (Skydio Onboard Modeling) and the product of a funded, acquisitive vendor with ATAK export (Reveal Farsight, USSOCOM-developed), the 3D Tiles rendering and basemap packaging are on TPC/AGC's 2026 agenda, algorithms are open (OpenDroneMap/Obj2Tiles), and the distribution half is covered by TAK Server sync, CloudTAK, map-depot, AGC RBT and Ditto. The residual increments could be shipped by TPC, Reveal, Skydio or Ditto within one or two release cycles (INFERENCE, MEDIUM). Analyst assessment: ACCEPTED at full strength; this session added two independent confirmations (UAS Tool KLV overlay; Reveal ATAK export + Series B) beyond what the parent skeptics cited.

feasibility.summary: Technically and legally the unclassified MVP is feasible for this team on $250k (open data, ATAK-CIV, commercial hardware, likely EAR99/ENC - counsel to confirm), which is why founder fit scores 3.5. The refutation is about founder fit to the market rather than to the build: three fatal-if-absent roles are missing, SBIR is blocked by the ownership test until restructuring and the German founder's permanent residency, TAK-GOV/MIL and CUI data are gated for the non-U.S.-person founder if the defense variant is pursued, and the credible customer milestone requires a sponsor the team does not have. Analyst assessment: ACCEPTED at strength 3; this lens is the weakest of the three because the scope was deliberately built to pass it.

score.verdict_rationale: Kill. Decisive reason: this narrower form is a feature set inside a government-owned, free, services-priced ecosystem, and its named functions are already delivered by the ecosystem's owner or its funded occupants. Verified this session: ATAK with the government UAS Tool plugin already overlays the KLV sensor footprint and stare point on the map (FACT, MEDIUM; UAS Tool user guide mirror and Play listing), and public-safety agencies are adopting exactly that free stack (HSToday); Skydio Onboard Modeling builds a 3D mesh on the controller within minutes and X10D streams to ATAK offline (company-reported, MEDIUM); Reveal Farsight produces 2D/3D at the edge 'in moments', exports to ATAK, was built with USSOCOM, partnered with Maxar (2025-05-06) and raised a $30M Series B with acquisition intent (MEDIUM); TPC's TAK Offsite 2026 agenda carries a Cesium 3D Tiles program update and an AGC Releasable Basemap Tiles demo (FACT, HIGH); OpenDroneMap plus Obj2Tiles make the imagery-to-3D-Tiles pipeline free (FACT, HIGH). The distribution half was already refuted in G03 (TAK Server sync, CloudTAK, map-depot, AGC RBT, Ditto) and nothing new rescues it. The PROBLEM -> USER -> REQUIREMENT OWNER -> PROGRAM OFFICE -> CONTRACTING OFFICE -> BUDGET -> VEHICLE path breaks at REQUIREMENT OWNER and BUDGET (no office owns the function; Public evidence insufficient for any line), which triggers the major penalty. The residual increments (edge change-vs-baseline overlays; bandwidth-budgeted priority delta of 3D terrain across non-NGC2 federations) are genuine but small, have no named buyer, and sit on roadmaps controlled by TPC, AGC, Reveal, Skydio and Ditto. Founder fit (3.5) is the best of the three cards in this lineage because the scope is unclassified by construction, but that is necessary, not sufficient: market attractiveness is 2.1 and the outcome ceiling is an acqui-hire or a TAK services shop. Competition skeptic strength 5, market 4, feasibility 3; I could not rebut any with evidence. Confidence MEDIUM: several key facts come from search summaries of company pages and a mirrored manual rather than primary documents read in full, and the hstoday fetch was blocked.
score.narrower_version_if_borderline: Not recommended as a company. If the founders insist on the space, the only rational use of capital is a 3-month, under-$30k validation: publish an open-source ATAK-CIV plugin that adds change-vs-baseline overlays to whatever 3D the user already has (Skydio/Reveal/ODM output), instrument adoption, interview five wildfire/SAR/S2 users and one TPC engineer, and ask one state TAK program or one allied civil-protection agency whether it would pay for support. If that produces a paid pilot, run it as a bootstrapped TAK plugin-and-services shop with Reveal, Skydio or a TAK integrator as the exit; if not, stop. Do not raise venture money against it and do not restructure the cap table for SBIR on the strength of this gap alone.
score.most_important_question_answer: If two exceptionally capable founders had $250,000 today and insisted on this gap, they should build only the piece nobody ships free: an open-source ATAK-CIV plugin plus a Jetson edge service that takes any MISB KLV feed or drone photo set, produces incremental 3D Tiles with OpenDroneMap-class tooling, and computes a change-vs-baseline overlay with a confidence slider against the previous flight or an open terrain baseline, delta-synced across two federated TAK Servers over an emulated 64 kbit/s link - roughly $60-150k and four to six months with one contracted photogrammetry engineer. They would show it to a wildfire incident-management-team situation unit that already runs ATAK (the CAL FIRE/IMT-4 type user), a state TAK program lead (COTAK-type), a brigade S2 12Y cell, and one TAK Product Center engineer. The demo would prove measured georegistration error against RTK, time-to-tiles per hectare on a Jetson, change-detection precision/recall on a staged scene, and bytes/time-to-converge versus native TAK mission packages after an outage. The customer would care because today change is judged by eye and 3D arrives hours later unless they own a Skydio or a Reveal licence. The honest answer to the crush test is that no incumbent needs to crush them: the government already owns the free vendor-neutral layer and has 3D Tiles and basemap packaging on its 2026 agenda, Skydio ships onboard 3D, and Reveal - funded, USSOCOM-born and openly acquisitive - can add change overlays to a product that already exports to ATAK; the founders' only protection is speed to a widely installed open plugin, which is a recruiting asset, not a company. The milestone that would justify $2-5M does not exist in a form this scope can reach: it would require a signed, paid pilot with a named requirement owner (a PM MC, USSOCOM, DHS S&T or allied solicitation naming change-vs-baseline or bandwidth-prioritised terrain distribution as a distinct requirement) plus written confirmation from TPC that neither function is on the ATAK or TAK Server roadmap. Because three research passes found neither, and because the buyer's revealed price for the surrounding stack is zero, this fails as a venture and survives at most as a bootstrapped plugin-and-services effort with an acqui-hire exit.
score.bear_case_summary: Every named function is free (ATAK UAS Tool KLV footprint), stock (Skydio Onboard Modeling), funded (Reveal Farsight with ATAK export, $33.6M STRATFI, $30M Series B, acquisitive), government-roadmapped (TPC Cesium 3D Tiles, AGC Releasable Basemap Tiles, TAK Server sync, CloudTAK) or open source (OpenDroneMap/Obj2Tiles); no requirement owner or budget line exists; public-safety users adopt free stacks; TAK plugin economics are services-shaped (PAR acquired by Booz Allen); the residual increments are one release cycle from four incumbents; and the team lacks the three fatal roles and an SBIR-eligible cap table.
score.bull_case_summary: The scope is fully unclassified, buildable on open data and commercial hardware in months, keeps both founders engaged, sits on a 500,000-user government-owned distribution channel with public source, and targets two functions (edge change-vs-baseline overlays; bandwidth-budgeted priority delta of 3D terrain across non-NGC2 and allied federations) that no fielded product is evidenced to deliver; OWT production and DFR expansion multiply the 3D data and the drone flights involved; allied TAK users and German civil protection are a channel the German founder can open; and Reveal's stated acquisition appetite gives a plausible, if small, exit.

verdicts.bear_case: There is no buyer. The user is real (drone operators, S2 cells, wildfire IMTs on ATAK) but the chain breaks immediately above them: no requirement owner names drone-agnostic sensor-to-map or bandwidth-budgeted terrain distribution, no program office owns it (TPC owns the client roadmap, AGC owns basemap packaging, DHS S&T owns the first-responder TAK program, PM IS&A owns Army edge exploitation via AIDP-Next), no contracting office buys plugins, and no budget line exists - the card itself records 'Public evidence insufficient'. Where money exists it is prime-shaped (AIDP-Next single award, TITAN production, NGC2 OTAs led by Anduril) or program-internal (DHS S&T paying integrators). Worse, the public-safety segment the parent skeptics pointed to has already revealed its price: agencies are adopting a fully free stack (ATAK + UAS Tool + MediaMTX) for drone video, and the KLV footprint overlay they get from it is the first function in this gap's title. The residual pains - change judged by eye, stale terrain packages - remained HYPOTHESIS/LOW after G03's two passes and this third pass found no AAR, solicitation or SOP naming them. The closest funded analogs (Reveal via STRATFI; Immersive Wisdom via a $25M-ceiling ordering contract; TAK services houses) are either SBIR-gated, which the cap table cannot pass today, or services-priced, which is consultancy drift by definition.
verdicts.strongest_single_argument: The government already owns the vendor-neutral, free layer this gap proposes to sell (TAK, UAS Tool, AGC Releasable Basemap Tiles, TAK Server sync), so the natural requirement owner is also the incumbent supplier; there is no office whose job is to buy this from a third party, and the public-safety buyer has shown it expects the footprint feature for free.

Capital is adequate for the PoC and inadequate for the 12-24 months of customer discovery needed to find a paying user inside a free ecosystem.

card.title: Software-only multi-node TDOA/AoA interference and rogue-emitter geolocation engine on commodity SDR nodes, plus an offline-first spectrum-management workflow client (JRFL/SFAF assignments, interference tickets) for installation, range and shared-band spectrum managers
card.problem: Installation, range and shared-band spectrum managers who receive an interference complaint still locate the source by sending a technician out with a handheld analyzer and then file the ticket by hand into DISA's online JSIR/Spectrum XXI tools, because affordable multi-node geolocation software and an offline-capable ticket/assignment client do not exist below the premium CRFS/Rohde & Schwarz/Keysight price tier.
echelons: test and training range frequency management office
brigade/division 25E spectrum manager (disconnected workflow use only)

user.exact_role: Installation spectrum manager (Army NEC/G6 installation spectrum manager; Air Force base spectrum manager under DAFI 17-221), range frequency manager, and unit 25E spectrum manager filing JSIR interference reports
user.echelon: installation / range / brigade
organization_examples: Army installation Network Enterprise Centers (NETCOM) and Army Spectrum Management Office
Air Force base communications squadrons (spectrum management per DAFI 17-221)
Test and training range frequency management offices (e.g., major Army/AF/Navy ranges - names not verified this session)
DISA Defense Spectrum Organization / Joint Spectrum Center (JSIR process owner)
CBRS SAS administrators and private-5G operators; FCC/NTIA enforcement (civil)

current_workflow: 1. Interference report arrives by phone, email or chat from a unit, tenant or neighbor.
2. Spectrum manager checks assignments in Spectrum XXI (mandated frequency request tool) and local records to see who is authorized on the frequency.
3. If the source is unknown, a technician drives out with a handheld analyzer (or a rented/loaned CRFS/R&S node) and manually direction-finds over hours to days.
4. Manager files or updates a JSIR report in JSIRO (Joint Spectrum Interference Resolution Online) per CJCSM 3320.02E; unresolved cases escalate to the Joint Spectrum Center.
5. For drone/rogue-emitter cases a separate C-UAS or passive-sensing stack (Hidden Level, Dedrone) with its own dashboard is consulted if the installation has one.
6. When disconnected (field CP, range, DDIL), assignments/JRFL and EMI tickets are kept in spreadsheets and re-entered later.
card.current_solution: Handheld analyzers plus drive-testing; premium fixed monitoring networks (CRFS RFeye with AoA/TDoA/PoA, Rohde & Schwarz hybrid AOA/TDOA systems, Keysight KSMS TDoA with three FieldFox units) where funded; Hidden Level passive-sensing networks now scaling over bases/ranges under a $100M-ceiling OTA; for Army tactical units S2AS (3dB Labs) which explicitly supports EMI resolution and warns of unauthorized interference sources; DISA enterprise tools (Spectrum XXI, JSIRO, JSDR, E2ESS, EMBM-J) for assignments and tickets; hobby/low-cost coherent DF (KrakenSDR with RDF Pro multi-station fusion) and small vendors such as Wavelet Lab offering multi-node SDR TDOA/FDOA platforms; spreadsheets when offline.
card.failure: It fails at two points: (a) below the premium tier there is no trusted, self-calibrating multi-node geolocation product an installation can afford for whole-base persistent coverage, so most sites do not geolocate at all and rely on drive tests; (b) the assignment/JRFL/JSIR workflow is enterprise-hosted (Spectrum XXI, JSIRO) and is not usable offline at ranges or field CPs, so data is re-keyed. Neither failure has a named requirement owner or budget line for a third-party software product; the funded responses (Hidden Level OTA, S2AS, REWSI sensors, EMBM-J recompete) are hardware-plus-software buys from already-selected vendors or DISA-captive tools.

card.why_existing_startups_havent_solved: They have, at every price point that has a paying buyer: premium vendors (CRFS, R&S, Keysight) sell hybrid AoA/TDoA systems to regulators, ranges and installations that can afford them; Hidden Level took the persistent base/range passive-sensing buyer under a $100M-ceiling OTA; 3dB Labs (S2AS) and the REWSI vendors (Heaviside, RII) took the Army tactical EMI-detection buyer with sensors bundled with software; Distributed Spectrum ($29M raised, AFRL SBIRs incl. localization algorithms) and Wavelet Lab already sell the low-cost-SDR-plus-software version; KrakenSDR ships RDF Pro. What remains - the sub-premium installation buyer with no sensor budget and the offline ticket client - is unsolved because that buyer has no requirement owner, program office or line (installation spectrum managers are records/compliance staff under NEC or the comm squadron), DISA DSO already owns the ticket workflow in JSIRO/EMBM-J, and the civil side is thin and price-sensitive (Aurora Insight precedent; CBRS interference is resolved by SAS administrators and measurement campaigns are run by NIST/ITS/MITRE).
card.technical_wedge: A hardware-free engine that turns 4-12 commodity coherent/GPSDO-synced SDR nodes (KrakenSDR/RTL-SDR/USRP class) into a self-calibrating TDOA+AoA geolocation service with honest per-fix CEP, multipath/false-alarm suppression tuned for dense installation RF, automatic matching of detections against an imported SFAF assignment list (authorized vs unauthorized), and a JSIR-format ticket generator; plus an offline-first client (web/WinTAK/ATAK-CIV plugin) that holds assignments, JRFL entries and tickets locally under DDIL and syncs to Spectrum XXI/JSIRO exports when connected. Explicitly excludes threat-emitter identification, EW/ES functions and any military-specific DF hardware to stay on the EAR side (needs counsel).

mvp.what: 6-node KrakenSDR/RTL-SDR+GPSDO network on a university campus or private land, a fusion service producing geolocations with CEP and confidence for cooperative ISM/amateur emitters, an SFAF-import authorized/unauthorized classifier using synthetic assignment data, and an offline JSIR-style ticket queue that syncs to a mock JSIRO export.
mvp.demonstrable_in_3_6_months: Yes: cooperative-emitter CEP curves over 1 km^2, time-to-locate under 30 minutes versus a manual drive test, ticket produced offline and synced after a simulated 60-minute outage.
mvp.what_it_must_prove: That cheap, imperfectly synchronized nodes reach a stated CEP (e.g., tens of meters) with a low false-fix rate in a dense campus RF environment; that a spectrum manager can produce a JSIR-format ticket offline faster than with spreadsheets; and - the hard part - that a named installation or range office will pay for it rather than wait for Hidden Level/S2AS/enterprise tools.

data_requirement.what: Multi-node time-synchronized IQ/detection recordings of installation-typical emitters (LMR, Wi-Fi, LTE/CBRS, ISM, GPS-jammer analogs where legal), site calibration data, SFAF-format assignment records, JRFL entries and JSIR ticket samples.
data_requirement.legally_realistically_obtainable: RF recordings: yes, self-collected on receive-only SDRs at a campus or with cooperative transmitters (FCC rules on content disclosure apply). SFAF/JSIR formats: public references (CJCSM 3320.02E, ATP 6-02.70) allow synthetic data. Real installation assignments, JRFL (may be classified) and JSIR records are CUI or classified and require a government sponsor; export-controlled CUI is effectively U.S.-person-only (E07-F30), so the Indonesian founder cannot handle it.

entry_vehicle.eligibility_notes: SBIR/STTR require >50% ownership and control by U.S. citizens or permanent residents (13 CFR 121.702; corpus E07-F3): the Indonesian founder's shares never count and the German founder's count only after the green card, so a 50/50 team fails unless the cap table is restructured (counsel). OTA/CSO/CRADA carry no citizenship test, but export-controlled CUI (assignments, JRFL, JSIR records) is effectively U.S.-person-only (E07-F30), so the Indonesian founder must be walled off from government data. Receive-only civil spectrum-monitoring software is plausibly EAR (5A001/5D001 or EAR99) rather than ITAR if it is not specially designed for military EW/DF - a commodity jurisdiction/classification review by counsel is required before design; ITAR treats the German founder as a U.S. person only on permanent residence (22 CFR 120.62).

regulatory_burden.explanation: Receive-only spectrum monitoring on COTS SDRs is legal domestically (FCC rules limit disclosure of intercepted content); a civil-scoped geolocation/workflow product that is not specially designed for military EW/DF is plausibly EAR (5A001/5D001 or EAR99) rather than USML Category XI, but direction-finding features aimed at military users can drift toward Category XI - only a commodity jurisdiction/classification review settles it. All real assignment, JRFL and JSIR data is CUI (JRFL may be classified), so any government pilot brings DFARS 252.204-7012/NIST SP 800-171/CMMC obligations. No clearance is needed for the civil product; a classified JRFL module would require a cleared facility and U.S.-citizen staff. None of this is a legal judgment.
regulatory_burden.non_us_person_founder_note: If the product stays EAR99/EAR-dual-use the Indonesian founder is largely unconstrained on the engine and client code (E07-F17), but must be excluded from export-controlled CUI supplied by any government sponsor (E07-F30) and cannot count toward SBIR ownership (13 CFR 121.702). The German founder becomes a U.S. person for ITAR only on permanent residence (22 CFR 120.62). A CFIUS filing could be triggered by foreign investors only if the product becomes ITAR/600-series critical technology (E07-F27). Needs export-control and immigration counsel before the first government conversation.

dual_use_potential.explanation: Civil buyers exist - private-5G/CBRS operators, telecom interference-hunting teams, airports and ports (GPS interference), event venues, regulators - and the shared-band policy push (NTIA Advanced DSS demonstration, NIST CBRS SEA program) keeps monitoring salient. But the civil market is thin and price-sensitive, CBRS interference is handled by SAS administrators and government measurement campaigns, premium vendors already serve regulators and telcos, and Aurora Insight is a documented failure of a standalone spectrum-data business. Medium, trending low for venture purposes.

defensibility.explanation: TDOA/AoA algorithms are published (R&S white paper, ION 2026 paper) and hardware is commodity, so code is not defensible. Per-site calibration data and a footprint of installed node networks would compound slowly; the JSIR/SFAF workflow client is copyable by DISA's contractors or the EWPMT-X integrator; government relationships (a CRADA, a DISA sponsor) would be the only real moat and are government-controlled. No network effects.

card.why_now: (1) Commodity coherent SDRs (KrakenSDR ~EUR 1,063) and GPSDO timing make sub-$2k geolocation nodes possible and peer-reviewed 2026 work shows jammer localization on low-cost arrays; (2) shared-spectrum policy (National Spectrum Strategy Advanced DSS demonstration at 3.1-3.45 GHz, NIST CBRS SEA measurements, GAO-26-107873) raises the salience of interference monitoring; (3) the Army proved in 2026 that cheap distributed spectrum sensors can be bought at production scale (REWSI) and that TAK is the tactical host (EWPMT-X), so an offline TAK-native client has a plausible home; (4) DISA is modernizing the enterprise stack (EMBM-J) and its SOSC support period runs to Sept 2026, a natural re-plan point. Counter: each of these has already pulled in a funded vendor or is being done in-house by government labs.
card.killer_risk: There is no buyer with signature authority and a budget for this scope: installation and range spectrum managers are compliance/records staff who buy handhelds, the persistent base/range sensing money went to Hidden Level (OTA), tactical EMI detection went to 3dB Labs/REWSI vendors, the ticket and assignment workflow is owned by DISA DSO (JSIRO, Spectrum XXI, EMBM-J recompete) which can add offline modes through its own contractors, and the civil market is thin and already served by R&S/CRFS/Keysight at the top and Distributed Spectrum/Wavelet Lab/KrakenSDR at the bottom - so the best case is a licensed feature or a small SaaS, not a company.

score.title: Software-only multi-node TDOA/AoA interference and rogue-emitter geolocation engine on commodity SDR nodes, plus an offline-first spectrum-management workflow client (JRFL/SFAF assignments, interference tickets) for installation, range and shared-band spectrum managers

scores.rationale: Interference at installations and ranges is a recurring operational nuisance that occasionally becomes mission-impacting (range ops halted, GPS interference, unauthorized emitters), and the doctrinal JSIR process exists precisely because of it (CJCSM 3320.02E, FACT MEDIUM); but it is not a survival issue and the funded responses (S2AS 'EMI resolution', Hidden Level base sensing) show the acute end is being addressed. 3.

EMI reporting and assignment work are continuous at every installation (DISA runs a five-year helpdesk contract for Spectrum XXI/JSIRO/JSDR/E2ESS, FACT MEDIUM) and every 25E works JRFL/assignments daily; but the specific event this product serves - an unknown emitter that must be geolocated - is episodic per site (INFERENCE, no frequency data found). 3.

Score 1 explained: FACT - no RDT&E/procurement line, program of record, SBIR topic, sources-sought or award exists for third-party installation interference-geolocation software or an offline spectrum-management client (this session's search and corpus E04-F31 both null). All adjacent money is committed to other vendors: Hidden Level $100M OTA ceiling (PR Newswire 2026-08-05), S2AS $350M ceiling (cpeisw 2026-06-01), REWSI ~$196M (DefenseScoop 2026-09-11), DISA EMBM-J recompete and SOSC support. Not 0 only because installation O&M does buy spectrum tools (handhelds, some CRFS/R&S nodes) and civil pilots are possible.

No CSO/OTA solicits this scope; DISA DSO is a captive buyer with incumbent contractors; installation purchases are micro-purchase/GSA-scale with no enterprise requirement owner; SBIR is closed to this cap table (13 CFR 121.702, FACT HIGH). OTA/CRADA paths exist in principle (E07-F28) and the Army showed non-traditionals can reach production fast (REWSI), which keeps this at 2 rather than 1.

TDOA/AoA geolocation on low-cost SDR arrays is published and demonstrated (NAVIGATION 2026 paper; R&S white paper; KrakenSDR/RDF Pro; Wavelet Lab), GPSDO timing is cheap, and the offline-first client is conventional engineering (CRDT sync, TAK plugin). Not 5 because calibration drift, multipath in dense installation RF and false-fix suppression at whole-base scale are real engineering risk on commodity nodes (INFERENCE, MEDIUM).
Software-only with bought-not-built nodes: PoC $40-120k fits founder capital with margin; a CRADA-scale pilot ($0.5-1.5M) does not, but $250k reaches a demonstrable product. 4.

A campus demo with CEP curves and an offline ticket queue is achievable in 3-6 months; a demo an installation or DISA JSC would credit requires site access and real (CUI) assignment data through a sponsor the founders do not have, pushing a credible demo to 9-15 months (INFERENCE). 3.

RF data is self-collectable on receive-only SDRs and the JSIR/SFAF formats are public enough for synthetic data; but real assignments, JRFL (may be classified) and JSIR records are CUI available only through a sponsor and not to the Indonesian founder (E07-F30, FACT MEDIUM). 3.

A civil-scoped, receive-only monitoring product is plausibly EAR rather than ITAR, no clearance is needed for the MVP, and encryption is a notification issue (E07-F32); but DF features marketed to military users can drift toward USML Category XI, CUI handling triggers DFARS 7012/CMMC, and SBIR ownership fails - all requiring counsel before design. Medium burden, 3.

The whole MVP is unclassified on commercial parts, open formats and synthetic assignment data. Not 5 because classification dependence is 'eventually': real JRFL entries can be classified, and installation emitter inventories are CUI from the first pilot.

Score 1 explained: every tier is occupied. Premium: R&S hybrid AOA/TDOA, CRFS RFeye AoA/TDoA/PoA, Keysight KSMS TDoA (vendor pages, FACT MEDIUM on existence). Funded base/range sensing: Hidden Level $100M OTA (FACT HIGH). Low-cost commodity-SDR software: Distributed Spectrum ($29M raised, AFRL SBIRs incl. localization algorithms, FACT MEDIUM), Wavelet Lab (FACT MEDIUM), KrakenSDR RDF Pro. Tactical EMI: 3dB Labs S2AS and REWSI vendors (FACT HIGH). Workflow: DISA JSIRO/Spectrum XXI/EMBM-J with Palantir and the GEMSIS contractor (FACT MEDIUM). Nothing is left uncontested.

Premium vendors are expensive and DISA's tools are legacy and online-only, which is a real soft spot; but Distributed Spectrum and Wavelet Lab already attack the low-cost seam, Hidden Level is freshly capitalized, and DISA can add offline modes through contractors it already pays. 2.

File-level SFAF import and CoT/TAK plugin output are open (FACT HIGH), and CBRS SAS interfaces are WInnForum-standard; but the systems of record that make the workflow client real - Spectrum XXI, JSDR, JSIRO, EMBM-J - have DISA-controlled, non-public interfaces, and installation C-UAS dashboards are vendor-controlled. A startup owns none of the military interfaces. 2.

Score 1 explained: the algorithms are public (R&S white paper; ION 2026 paper), the hardware is commodity, an open-source floor (KrakenSDR/Heimdall/RDF Pro) exists, and the workflow client is copyable by DISA's or PM EW&C's existing contractors. The only compounding assets - per-site calibration footprint and a government sponsor relationship - are small and government-controlled. No network effects.

Real civil buyers exist (private-5G/CBRS operators, telcos, airports/ports for GPS interference, regulators) and shared-band policy keeps monitoring salient (NTIA Advanced DSS demonstration; NIST CBRS SEA program, FACT MEDIUM); but the civil market is thin and price-sensitive, CBRS interference is handled by SAS administrators and government labs, premium vendors already serve it, and Aurora Insight is a failure precedent (FACT MEDIUM). 3.

Adjacent expansions run straight into killed or occupied lanes: sensor-agnostic EM COP fusion (parent G11, killed), C-UAS RF layer (Hidden Level/Anduril), enterprise spectrum management (DISA/Palantir), allied regulators (R&S/CRFS home turf). The user base (installation/range spectrum managers plus a few thousand 25Es) is small. 2.

A per-site subscription with recurring ticket volume and node additions is plausible and civil SaaS could renew annually; but per-site contract value is small (tens of thousands at most, INFERENCE) and government sustainment would flow through an integrator's vehicle. 3.

This is the most founder-accessible form in the G21/G11 family: software-only, commercial hardware, plausibly EAR-scoped so the Indonesian founder can work on the core, $250k sufficient for the PoC, and a strong engineer plus a product/finance founder can build it. Missing but recruitable: an RF/DSP array-calibration engineer, a former spectrum-manager advisor and export counsel (three fatal-if-absent roles). SBIR is closed and CUI must be walled off. The fit is good for building the product and poor for reaching a buyer with signature authority. 3.

market.summary: No requirement owner, program office, line or vehicle exists for this scope; the persistent base/range sensing money went to Hidden Level (OTA), tactical EMI detection to 3dB Labs/REWSI vendors, and the ticket/assignment workflow is owned by DISA DSO (JSIRO, Spectrum XXI, EMBM-J recompete) which can add offline modes via its own contractors; installation spectrum managers are records/compliance staff with micro-purchase authority; the civil shared-band side is served by SAS administrators and NIST/ITS/MITRE measurement programs and carries the Aurora Insight failure precedent. The chain breaks at REQUIREMENT OWNER, PROGRAM OFFICE, BUDGET and VEHICLE - major penalty applies.

competition.summary: The geolocation engine is commodity: R&S, CRFS and Keysight publish and sell hybrid AOA/TDOA systems; Wavelet Lab and KrakenSDR RDF Pro already sell software-on-commodity-SDR fusion; Distributed Spectrum ($29M, AFRL SBIRs incl. localization algorithms) sits exactly on the low-cost seam with DoD relationships; Hidden Level holds the base/range OTA. The workflow client is copyable by the GEMSIS/EMBM-J contractors (incl. Palantir) or the EWPMT-X integrator on the government's request. No incumbent needs six months - most already have it.

feasibility.summary: The narrow form is genuinely buildable and demonstrable for under $120k on commercial parts, plausibly EAR-scoped so the non-U.S.-person founder can work on the core (counsel required) - so feasibility does not kill it. What refutes it is access: a credible demo needs an installation or DISA sponsor and CUI assignment/JSIR data that the founders cannot obtain and the Indonesian founder cannot touch, SBIR is closed by ownership, and the only reachable buyers (civil pilots, an OEM license) cap the outcome at a small business. Strength 3: it survives as a consultancy/feature path, not as a company.

score.verdict_rationale: Kill as a venture, with the major chain penalty applied: PROBLEM -> USER is intact (interference at installations/ranges is real and the JSIR process is doctrinal), but REQUIREMENT OWNER, PROGRAM OFFICE, BUDGET and VEHICLE do not exist for third-party interference-geolocation software or an offline spectrum client (null search this session; corpus E04-F31 null), and every adjacent funded buyer is already occupied - Hidden Level ($100M OTA ceiling, 2026-07-30) for base/range passive sensing, 3dB Labs S2AS ($350M ceiling, 2026-06-01, explicitly covering EMI resolution) and REWSI vendors (~$196M, Aug-Sep 2026) for tactical spectrum, DISA DSO (JSIRO, Spectrum XXI, EMBM-J SA recompete) for the workflow of record. The technology is commodity (R&S/CRFS/Keysight at the top; Distributed Spectrum, Wavelet Lab and KrakenSDR RDF Pro at the bottom; ION 2026 paper shows the algorithms are public), so potential moat scores 1 and competitive intensity 1. Market attractiveness 2.3 is below the bar even though founder fit 3.3 is the best in the G21/G11 family - the team can build it but nobody with signature authority is set up to buy it, which is the definition of a consultancy/feature path. Decisive reason: no buyer with a budget and vehicle for this scope, and the price-and-usability seam it targets is already contested by funded low-cost vendors. Scores are heuristics, not facts.
score.narrower_version_if_borderline: Not borderline. For the record, the only residual that could pay its way is a services/IP-licensing business: (a) license the self-calibrating TDOA/AoA fusion module to a sensor OEM or integrator that lacks it, or (b) build the offline JSIR/SFAF client as an open ATAK-CIV plugin under a CRADA with one installation or DISA JSC and sell sustainment as a subcontractor - explicitly not venture-scale.
score.most_important_question_answer: If two exceptionally capable founders spent $250,000 on G32 today, they should build nothing custom in hardware: buy six KrakenSDR/RTL-SDR nodes with GPSDO timing, write the self-calibrating TDOA/AoA fusion service with honest per-fix CEP and a false-fix model tuned on a dense campus RF environment, add an SFAF-import authorized/unauthorized classifier and an offline JSIR-format ticket queue as an ATAK-CIV/WinTAK plugin, and spend under $120k doing it. They should show it first to one Air Force base spectrum manager and one Army installation NEC spectrum manager reached through a National Guard or ROTC relationship, and in parallel to one private-5G/CBRS operator and one test-range frequency office, and second to a sensor OEM (Distributed Spectrum, Heaviside, Hidden Level) as a licensable module. The demo would prove that cheap, imperfectly synchronized nodes locate a cooperative emitter to a stated CEP in under 30 minutes versus hours of drive-testing, and that a ticket can be produced offline and synced later. The customer would care because a technician's day is the current cost of every unknown-emitter complaint and because Spectrum XXI/JSIRO are online-only. But the honest answer is that an incumbent does not need to crush them: R&S, CRFS and Keysight already sell the capability and can add a lite tier; Distributed Spectrum and Wavelet Lab already sell the low-cost version; DISA can add offline modes through the contractors it already pays; and the installation spectrum manager who loves the demo cannot sign more than a micro-purchase. The milestone that would justify $2-5M is either an enterprise agreement from IMCOM/AFIMSC or DISA DSO designating the offline client, or an OTA from PM EW&C or OUSW(R&E) naming the fusion module, or more than $1M ARR from civil sites - and none of those owners has signalled the requirement. Absent that signal within 12 months, it fails, and the $250,000 should go to a gap where the founders can own a seam a program office is actually funding.
score.bear_case_summary: No requirement owner, program office, budget line, SBIR topic or vehicle exists for this scope; the adjacent money is committed to Hidden Level (OTA), 3dB Labs (S2AS, which explicitly covers EMI resolution), REWSI vendors and DISA's own tool contractors; the geolocation algorithms are published and sold at every price tier (R&S/CRFS/Keysight; Distributed Spectrum; Wavelet Lab; KrakenSDR RDF Pro); the workflow client is copyable by DISA/EWPMT-X contractors; the installation user has no signature authority; the civil market is thin with the Aurora Insight precedent; the cap table fails SBIR and CUI must be walled from the non-U.S.-person founder; potential moat 1, competitive intensity 1. Three skeptics refute at strengths 4, 4 and 3.
score.bull_case_summary: The pain is real and doctrinal (JSIR process; DISA running a five-year support contract for online-only tools), the user exists at every installation and range, cheap coherent SDRs and a 2026 peer-reviewed low-cost jammer-localization result make the engine buildable, the MVP is fully unclassified and within founder capital, the product can plausibly be scoped to EAR so the Indonesian founder can work on the core, shared-band policy (NTIA Advanced DSS demonstration, NIST CBRS SEA, GAO-26-107873) keeps interference monitoring salient, and the Army proved in 2026 that cheap spectrum sensors get bought at production scale. This adds up to a credible small software business or licensable module, not a venture-scale company.

verdicts.bear_case: G32 has a user but no buyer. Installation and base spectrum managers are compliance and records staff inside a NEC or communications squadron (DAFI 17-221; CJCSM 3320.02E) whose purchasing authority is a handheld analyzer, not a whole-base sensor network or a new workflow system; range frequency offices sit inside range infrastructure vehicles held by primes (e.g., the Space Force $981M test/training IDIQ, 2026-07-31). The money that does exist for the problem was committed in 2026 to already-selected vendors: OUSW(R&E)'s $100M-ceiling OTA to Hidden Level for passive sensing over bases, ranges and border (2026-07-30), the Army's $350M-ceiling S2AS production to 3dB Labs whose stated scope includes EMI resolution and warning of unauthorized interference sources (2026-06-01), and ~$196M of REWSI spectrum-sensor production (Aug-Sep 2026). The ticket and assignment workflow is government-owned by DISA DSO - Spectrum XXI is the mandated tool, JSIRO is the ticket system, a SOSC helpdesk contract runs to Sept 2026 and the EMBM-J SA recompete is in flight - so an offline client has a single captive buyer that can order offline modes from contractors it already pays. On the civil side, CBRS interference is resolved by SAS administrators, shared-band measurement is done by NIST/ITS/NASA/MITRE under NASCTN (NIST, Sept 2026), and Aurora Insight is the precedent for a standalone spectrum-data business failing to scale. No SBIR/STTR, DIU, AFWERX or CSO topic for this scope surfaced (this session; corpus E04-F31). The result is consultancy drift: the only revenue shapes are pilots, CRADAs and licensed modules.
verdicts.strongest_single_argument: The PROBLEM -> USER chain ends at the user: no requirement owner, program office, budget line or vehicle exists for third-party installation interference-geolocation software or an offline spectrum client, and every adjacent funded buyer (Hidden Level OTA, S2AS, REWSI, DISA DSO tools) is already committed to another vendor as of Sept 2026.

verdicts.narrower_survivable_version: A subcontract/licensing business: supply the TDOA/AoA fusion module to a sensor OEM or the EMBM-J/EWPMT-X integrator, or build the offline JSIR client under a CRADA and sell sustainment - a small services company, not a venture.

verdicts.bear_case: The gap assumes the geolocation software is the missing piece, but it is the most commoditized piece. Rohde & Schwarz publishes a hybrid AOA/TDOA white paper and sells modular, scalable systems; Keysight's KSMS runs TDoA on three synchronized FieldFox handhelds an installation may already own; CRFS RFeye arrays do AoA, TDoA and PoA; and a 2026 NAVIGATION paper shows jammer/spoofer localization on a low-cost SDR array, so the algorithms are public. At the bottom of the market KrakenRF ships RDF Pro multi-station fusion with a ~EUR 1,063 node and Wavelet Lab already sells a multi-node SDR TDOA/FDOA geolocation platform - the exact 'software on commodity SDR' proposition. In the middle, Distributed Spectrum has raised ~$29M (Series A Mar 2025, Conviction/Shield Capital), positions on commodity hardware plus algorithms, held an AFRL SBIR Phase II for low-SWaP RF SA and an SBIR to improve transmitter localization on its low-cost SDR network, and holds DoD relationships a student team lacks. Hidden Level holds the base/range OTA and can license its processing onto cheaper nodes. For the workflow client, DISA's contractors (the GEMSIS sustainment vendor; Palantir for EMBM-J DS) and the Army's EWPMT-X integrator own the systems of record and their non-public APIs; an offline JRFL/JSIR mode is a capability drop for them, and the government prefers to own TAK components. Switching cost for a spectrum manager is nil because the startup would import/export the same SFAF/JSIR files as everyone else. Anduril, Palantir and L3Harris do not need to add it; smaller, already-funded vendors already have.
verdicts.strongest_single_argument: Every price tier of the proposed product already has a seller - R&S/CRFS/Keysight at the top, Distributed Spectrum ($29M, DoD SBIRs on localization) and Hidden Level ($100M OTA) in the funded middle, Wavelet Lab and KrakenSDR RDF Pro at the bottom - and the workflow client's systems of record (Spectrum XXI, JSIRO, EMBM-J, EWPMT-X) are owned by DISA/PM EW&C contractors who can add offline modes on request.

verdicts.bear_case: This is the one form in the G21/G11 family the team can actually build: no hardware to manufacture, commodity SDRs at ~EUR 1,000 per node, published algorithms, an unclassified MVP under $120k, and a product that - if scoped to civil receive-only monitoring without military DF/EW features - is plausibly EAR rather than ITAR so the Indonesian founder can work on the core (counsel must confirm; E07-F16/F17). Feasibility therefore does not kill it. Access does. A demo that an installation or DISA JSC would credit needs a real base site, real SFAF assignments and real JSIR records, all CUI (JRFL possibly classified), obtainable only through a sponsor the founders do not have and handled only by U.S.-person staff under DFARS 7012/NIST 800-171 - so the non-U.S.-person co-founder is excluded from exactly the data that makes the product real (E07-F30). SBIR/STTR, the natural $150k-$1.5M bridge, is closed unless the cap table is restructured (13 CFR 121.702). The founders' first customers are therefore civil pilots and OEM licenses, both of which cap the company at a small business; a five-year procurement cycle is not the issue because there is no procurement to wait for. The MVP is under $100k, but the credible-demo stage ($0.5-1.5M) requires the sponsor relationship and U.S.-person hires the team lacks.
verdicts.strongest_single_argument: The team can build and legally demonstrate the civil-scoped engine for under $120k, but the data and site access that would make it credible to a military buyer are CUI held by sponsors the founders cannot reach and cannot share with the non-U.S.-person co-founder, and the SBIR bridge is closed by ownership - so feasibility confirms a small-business path and refutes a venture path.

card.title: Independent track-provenance and after-action audit tool for C-UAS and unit drone operations, with a friendly-flight declaration adapter (MAVLink/GCS to CoT flight-intent extension) and an offline-first UAS operator/airframe qualification and readiness ledger
card.problem: After a counter-UAS engagement or a unit drone mission nobody can independently reconstruct which sensor said what, when, and why a track was called friend or unknown; friendly drone intent still reaches the C-UAS picture by voice and hand-marking; and units fielding thousands of multi-vendor drones track operator qualification and airframe readiness in DTMS entries, spreadsheets and binders.

user.exact_role: (a) JIATF-401 and JICO/ADAM-cell oversight staff, CTC observer-controller-trainers and range control officers who review C-UAS engagements and airspace incidents after the fact; (b) battalion S3 air NCOs and company drone team leaders who must declare friendly flights; (c) battalion sUAS master trainers and S3 sections who maintain operator/airframe readiness records
user.echelon: company to brigade for (b) and (c); CTC, range and joint-task-force oversight for (a)
organization_examples: JIATF-401 (DoD C-sUAS lead, established 2025-08-28)
Transformation-in-Contact battalions (e.g., 2-35 IN / 25th ID; 4ID units)
JPMRC / JMRC / NTC observer-controller airspace cells (the community that wrote CALL Handbook 25-14)
Yuma Proving Ground / Falcon Peak exercise control (NORTHCOM, JIATF-401)
3rd Combat Aviation Brigade airspace management cell (BARS marking workaround)

current_workflow: 1. Friendly drone launch announced by radio/chat; unit marks it by BARS (bearing, altitude, range, speed) or an ATAK point; ADAM/BAE cell deconflicts procedurally per CALL 25-14 altitude blocks and ROZs
2. C-UAS sensors publish tracks into FAAD C2 or Lattice; operator correlates with the announced friendly flights under time pressure and labels friend/unknown/hostile

3. After an engagement, near-miss or exercise serial, the O/C-T or oversight staff rebuild the timeline from vendor screen recordings, radio logs, TAK chat and memory; the C2 vendor's own replay (where it exists) is the only machine record

4. Lessons learned are written into AARs and, at joint level, into products such as the JIATF-401 2026 Quick Reference Guide; no cross-vendor, government-owned machine-readable provenance record is retained

5. Operator qualification (sUAS Master Trainer course completions, currency), airframe and battery status are recorded in DTMS course-completion entries, unit spreadsheets, vendor clouds (Skydio Cloud) and paper logs; readiness is reported by hand
card.current_solution: Lattice (JIATF-401 common tactical C-UAS C2, $87M task order Mar 2026) and FAAD C2 with their built-in track logs and vendor-specific replay; TAK/ATAK with the free government UAS Tool plugin (MAVLink-class drones appear as CoT with telemetry and FMV); Auterion Mission Control CoT-to-ATAK feeds; procedural airspace control (CALL 25-14) and BARS hand-marking; DTMS as the Army system of record for individual training records; commercial fleet/compliance tools (AirData, Aloft, DroneSense - public-safety oriented); government test organizations and FFRDC data-collection teams at C-UAS test events (RECALL - not re-verified this session).
card.failure: Three distinct failures: (a) there is no vendor-neutral, government-owned provenance record that survives the exercise or engagement - the only machine record lives inside the C2 vendor's stack, so oversight staff cannot independently grade fusion quality or explain a friend/unknown call; (b) friendly-flight intent (window, geometry, purpose) is not encoded in the CoT the C-UAS picture consumes, so blue-ID collapses to voice and pattern-matching; (c) operator currency and airframe readiness across Skydio/Auterion/Gauntlet fleets have no unit-owned offline ledger, so readiness is re-typed by hand. The narrow form deliberately excludes live fusion and live friend/foe identification.

card.why_existing_startups_havent_solved: Because each of the three pieces is either already given away or already owned. The MAVLink-to-CoT bridge ships free in the government TAK UAS Tool and in Auterion's CoT feed, so no startup can charge for it; a flight-intent extension to CoT is a schema decision that belongs to the TAK Product Center and JIATF-401, not to a vendor. Operator/airframe records have a mandated home (DTMS) plus vendor clouds and mature commercial compliance tools, so a unit ledger is a spreadsheet replacement nobody budgets for. The independent after-action audit is the one function with real oversight value, and it is precisely the one startups cannot reach: the machine records live inside Lattice/FAAD C2 (CUI, vendor formats), the government already staffs independent measurement through test organizations and FFRDC data-collection teams at events like Falcon Peak (RECALL - not re-verified this session), and the customer's revealed preference in Sept 2026 was to make the incumbent stack itself the measurement baseline. Absence of a startup here reflects absence of a buyer, not an overlooked seam.
card.technical_wedge: A single ATAK-CIV plugin plus a small offline-first edge service that (1) emits a 'friendly-flight declaration' CoT event (proposed schema extension: flight window, launch point, altitude block/ROZ geometry, purpose, operator ID) generated from a MAVLink GCS or hand entry and pre-checks it against unit-authored ACMs; (2) records every incoming track/CoT event with source, timestamp and label into a tamper-evident local log that syncs opportunistically; and (3) replays and diffs those logs after a serial to show which source reported which track, when, and what the friendly declaration said at that moment. The audit engine is sensor-agnostic and could later ingest exported Lattice/FAAD C2 logs if a sponsor grants them.

mvp.what: ATAK-CIV plugin + edge service on a laptop/Android: friendly-flight declaration from a PX4/ArduPilot GCS, a unit ledger (operators, currency, airframes, batteries) that works offline and syncs via TAK Server, and an after-action replay that reconstructs a scripted range serial from 2-3 commercial sensor feeds (low-cost radar or RF detector, EO camera tracker, Remote ID/ADS-B receiver) with per-source lineage.
mvp.demonstrable_in_3_6_months: Yes for all three pieces on self-collected range data with 3-5 commercial drones and 50-200 synthetic tracks; roughly 8-12 weeks for adapter+ledger, 4-6 months to add the replay/audit engine. Cost roughly $40-90k including hardware.
mvp.what_it_must_prove: That (a) a declared friendly flight can be matched to a detected track with measurable precision/recall when cooperative signals are removed, (b) the replay reconstructs a labelled timeline that an O/C-T would accept as evidence, (c) the ledger replaces spreadsheet/binder tracking without a network - and, critically, that a named government sponsor will supply real exercise logs, without which the demo proves only that the plumbing works.

data_requirement.what: Track/CoT event logs from C-UAS C2 (source, time, label, confidence), friendly-flight declarations and GCS telemetry, unit ACMs/ACOs, and operator/airframe/battery/qualification records; for a credible military demo, exported engagement logs from Lattice/FAAD C2 and exercise ground truth.
data_requirement.legally_realistically_obtainable: MVP: yes - self-generated MAVLink telemetry, commercial c-UAS sensor outputs, Remote ID/ADS-B, synthetic ACMs built from FM 3-52/CALL 25-14, synthetic personnel records. Credible demo: only through a sponsor (JIATF-401, a CTC, ATEC/test organization) - engagement logs are CUI at minimum and vendor-format; real unit training records contain PII; export-controlled CUI is effectively US-person-only (E07-F30), so the Indonesian co-founder cannot be assumed to handle that half. Needs counsel.

incumbent_response.could_anduril_palantir_l3harris_add_it: Yes for two of three pieces within a release cycle: Lattice/FAAD C2 can expose track lineage, replay and a blue-drone declaration ingest as features (they own the data and the JIATF-401 relationship); the TAK Product Center can add a flight-intent field to the UAS Tool. incumbent_response.why_startup_still_wins_or_reject: Reject as a standalone company thesis. The adapter and ledger are features with a $0 government baseline; the audit is a services/test-support role whose data the startup cannot access without a sponsor and whose institutional owner (government testers) already exists. A startup could win a small pilot on speed and unit goodwill, but nothing here compounds into a defensible product.

regulatory_burden.explanation: The adapter and ledger on ATAK-CIV with commercial drones are low-burden (EAR99-level per E07; PII handling if real personnel data is used). Burden rises sharply for the audit half: C-UAS engagement logs and Lattice/FAAD C2 interface formats are CUI and likely export-controlled; exercise captures may be classified; government plugin signing and an ATO under a host system are needed for fielded use; CMMC self-assessment applies once on contract. Not a legal judgment.
regulatory_burden.non_us_person_founder_note: The Indonesian founder can build and demo the adapter and ledger today. The audit engine's real data (export-controlled CUI) is effectively US-person-only (E07-F30); ITAR technical data has no deemed-export exception for domestic foreign-person employees (E07-F18); a technology control plan and counsel review are needed before the first sponsor data set. The German founder's expected permanent residency resolves US-person status for export purposes but not clearance eligibility. Any allied (Bundeswehr) deployment could constitute an ITAR 'defense service' even for EAR99 software (E07-F15). Needs counsel.

dual_use_potential.explanation: Civil C-UAS sites (airports, stadiums, prisons, DHS/FAA test sites) need incident forensics and public-safety drone programs need currency/compliance ledgers, and both are fully unclassified - but those markets are already served by SkySafe/D-Fend/Dedrone forensics and AirData/Aloft/DroneSense compliance tools consolidating under Versaterm, so the dual-use beachhead is crowded rather than open.

defensibility.explanation: No data moat (logs belong to the government or the C2 vendor), no algorithm moat (replay/diff and record-matching are commodity), no interface moat (TPC, Anduril, Northrop and drone OEMs own every interface). At best a unit-adopted workflow and an O/C-T relationship - both non-transferable and non-compounding.

card.why_now: Friendly-drone density exploded (12,080 Gauntlet drones by Sept 2026, drones-to-every-squad), CALL 25-14 and BARS hand-marking document the procedural workaround, the $87M Lattice task order under a $20B enterprise agreement and Falcon Peak 26.2's 'baseline standard' role create lock-in anxiety that an independent record would answer, the Army CTO's NGC2 memo and DoD IG's Advana audit put logging/audit gaps on record, and ATAK-CIV plus the free UAS Tool make the plumbing trivial to build. What has not changed is that nobody has funded any of it.
card.killer_risk: There is no PROBLEM -> REQUIREMENT OWNER -> PROGRAM OFFICE -> BUDGET -> VEHICLE path for any of the three pieces: the adapter duplicates a free government plugin and a schema the TAK Product Center controls; the ledger duplicates DTMS and mature commercial compliance tools; and the audit function - the only part with oversight value - depends on export-controlled logs the founders cannot access and on an independence role the government already fills with its own test organizations and FFRDCs, so the best outcome is an unfunded pilot or a test-support services engagement, not a company.
